items.feedback_item: The folded suitcase cannot contain the one-piece backbone and the tri-star clusters as claimed.
items.must_change: The solution claims a folded envelope of 730 by 380 by 190 mm for 52.7 L (E42) with 390 mm door clearance in the van door (E76) while also defining the backbone as two one-piece 1100 mm tubes with sliding handle in fabrication step 1. A 1100 mm bar cannot stow in a 730 mm length, and a 370 mm overall cluster diameter from 110 mm centre radius plus 75 mm wheel radius cannot be inferred to fit in 190 mm thickness without a stacked-dimension sketch, and the 365 mm toe-plate width plus outboard clusters are not summed across the claimed 380 mm width. What is true is that the van space read from opened pages (E36) is real but the summation of parts into that space was never shown. What must change is a dimensioned stacked folded layout that sums backbone length, handle overlap, cluster diameter and thickness, and toe-plate width, or a redesign to a two-piece or telescoping backbone that actually achieves the claimed length. Why it matters is van stow with one-person handling is a primary constraint and the device cannot be accepted on hope that the suitcase fits.

items.feedback_item: The braced backbone stiffness claim uses the wrong structural model and understates deflection by about eight times.
items.must_change: The solution correctly computes unbraced cantilever tip deflection from delta equals F times L cubed divided by 3 times E times I with half weight 294.5 N on 1.1 m and tube inertia 1.73e-08 m4 (E69) to about 0.11 m (E71). It then claims 13.8 mm braced deflection by multiplying by 0.5 cubed (E85), which is the formula for halving the cantilever span to a new ground support. What is actually true is that a transverse clip across the two tubes does not ground the midspan in fore-aft bending where both tubes already bend together, so the model is outside its regime and the deployed deflection remains near 110 mm. What must change is to remove the 13.8 mm claim, keep 110 mm as the deployed whip unless the brace is redesigned as a stayed or triangulated support to ground, and re-evaluate handling and cluster alignment on the 197 mm riser (E16). Why it matters is 110 mm whip changes stair nose contact and operator control.

items.feedback_item: The parcel offset and backbone stress use two different moments for the same load and the impact factor has no calculation.
items.must_change: The solution correctly computes parcel weight from W equals m times g with 60 kg giving about 589 N (E7) and toe root moment from M equals W times a with 589 N at 0.15 m giving 88.3 N m (E68). It then computes backbone bending stress from sigma equals M times y divided by I with 589 N at 0.20 m shared by two tubes to about 51.1 MPa per tube (E70) using the correct tube inertia (E69), and static safety factor 276 divided by 51.1 equals 5.4 (E74) for the higher moment. What is actually true is both 51.1 MPa and 5.4 are correct arithmetic for the 0.20 m input but inconsistent with the 0.15 m offset used for the toe moment, so traceability is broken. What must change is to pick one parcel centre, reuse it for toe moment and backbone stress, recompute stress and static factor, and add the missing impact calculation if the claimed 3.60 with impact is retained. Why it matters is the frame is sized from this moment. The axle torsion from tau equals 16 times T divided by pi times d cubed with 33.5 N m on 20 mm diameter giving about 21.3 MPa (E88) and the toe-pin single shear from tau equals F divided by A with 294.5 N on an 8 mm pin giving about 5.86 MPa (E89) recompute as correct and need no change.

items.feedback_item: The stair torque is used inconsistently as total and per-side and the brake sizing follows from the unsettled number.
items.must_change: The solution reports pivot torque about 38.8 N m per side with 188 N descent hold and 24 N flat push in the climb simulation (E23) and separately 67.0 N m locked torque from slope times 0.185 m radius (E51). What is actually true from a check with total weight 652 N for 66.7 kg on stair angle arctan of 0.197 divided by 0.254 equals 37.8 deg from the IRC limits (E16, E24) is slope load about 400 N and total torque about 66.6 N m, so 67.0 N m total is plausible but 39.0 N m per side would be 78 N m total and does not agree with 67.0 N m. What must change is to settle total versus per-side definition, correct the 209 N pull and 188 N hold and 67.0 N m lock to one consistent free-body, and resize caliper clamp and tooth pin from the corrected total. Why it matters is the disc plus tooth park lock is the safety-critical holding means.

items.feedback_item: The climb work understates the lifted mass by about ten percent.
items.must_change: The solution correctly computes lift energy from E equals m times g times h with 60 kg through 0.197 m giving about 116 J per riser (E22). What is actually true is the operator lifts the total lifted mass of 66.7 kg from parcel plus tare plus brace (E86, E41, E73) for about 129 J, so the board understates climb work by about ten percent. What must change is to replace 116 J with the total-mass energy in the constraint table and stair simulation and carry the total weight into slope and torque numbers. Why it matters is work, pull, and holding torque all scale with the mass actually lifted on the 197 mm riser.

items.feedback_item: The single-operator holding case exceeds sustained hand limits and rests entirely on an uncalculated spring-applied lock with weak human-factor sources.
items.must_change: The solution shows stair pull 209 N and descent hold 188 N in the simulation (E23) against sustained limits with ratio 188 divided by 130 equals 1.45 (E59), and correctly sizes van restraint from 0.8 times tare weight for 51 N (E67) on the steepest IRC stair (E16, E24). What is actually true is the dynamic pull numbers exceed one-hand sustained capability, so the safety case rests entirely on the spring-applied disc plus tooth lock holding the largest slope load of about 400 N while released, and the lever-force and cold tired-hand limits on the board rest on search results whose pages were never opened (E77, E78, E79), which is weaker than values read from opened pages. What must change is to replace unopened sources with opened sources and add calculable lever mechanical advantage, cable loss, required finger force to release and meter, and holding margin with impact for the locked 400 N slope case instead of deferring to bench test. Why it matters is hands-off holding on stairs is the claimed novelty over fixed skid trucks and cannot be accepted without a force margin.

process_cause: The meeting did form proposal v2 and collected ready votes from all four members after four cycles with no open objections, so the rejection is not from a missing proposal or an unresolved objection. The process cause is voting ready before the deciding quantities were reconciled: the dimensional stack for the 730 mm suitcase, the total versus per-side torque definition, and the brace deflection model were left inconsistent, and the tired-hand lever and tooth engagement were deferred to built-hardware bench test that concept review must not depend on for acceptance.
summary: The tri-star walking principle on a twin-tube backbone with spring-applied disc plus tooth lock is physically sound, buildable, and a credible step beyond fixed-frame 60 kg stair trucks, but it cannot go to detail design until the folded geometry is summed or redesigned, the brace is remodeled from 13.8 mm to near 110 mm or re-designed as a stayed support, and the parcel offset, total mass energy, and total versus per-side torque are made consistent with a calculated lever holding margin.
